periods.analysis: Budget Variance finished 2024-Q3 at 2.1%, green against the <=3.0% control target and a sound baseline for this eight-quarter run. With no prior quarter in this series, I am treating 2.1% as the starting control point rather than a trend signal. The variance was concentrated in predictable places: summer parks staffing, marina security overtime on Route H-17 events, and delayed encumbrances for the FinanceOne reporting module. For a fast-growing AA-rated city, this is the right kind of narrow variance: visible, documented, and not masking structural pressure.
periods.recommendations: Keep the monthly Budget Control Review in place, with department-level variance explanations due by the fifth business day after close. Extend the green performance by adding a Q4 encumbrance scrub for purchase orders over $75,000, especially in Parks, Public Works, and IT. Finance should also lock a standard variance-code list in Munis so explanations are comparable across departments.

periods.analysis: Budget Variance improved to 1.9% in 2024-Q4, down 0.2 percentage points from 2.1%, and remained green. The year-end close benefited from tighter purchase-order liquidation, particularly the cancellation of stale POs tied to facilities work orders FV-4421 through FV-4438. Departments also responded well to the Q3 control message; late journal entries were fewer and better supported. This is a favorable close, but I would not call it self-sustaining without the same discipline in the first-quarter reset.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the Q4 result by making the stale-PO review a formal year-end checklist item owned jointly by Purchasing and Budget. Extend the control to open grant-funded projects, where timing differences can look harmless until reimbursement files lag. For 2025-Q1, require every department with variance above 2.0% to submit a one-page variance bridge before the quarterly forecast is certified.

periods.analysis: Budget Variance moved to 2.1% in 2025-Q1, up 0.2 percentage points from 1.9%, still green and comfortably inside the <=3.0% target. The increase is consistent with the first-quarter pattern: new salary schedules, insurance renewals, and early-year contract mobilization before full revenue timing is visible. The largest timing items were fleet fuel hedging entries and the onboarding costs for the Harborview Service Center permit counter expansion. Controls are holding, but the quarter reminds us that growth creates small timing risks before it creates obvious budget risk.
periods.recommendations: Keep the green position by running a Q1 personnel-cost true-up using actual filled positions rather than adopted headcount assumptions. Extend the forecast discipline to all new operating initiatives approved in the budget, with Finance assigning each a control ID and quarterly spend curve. I also recommend a targeted review of fuel, insurance, and software renewals before the Q2 forecast is published.

periods.analysis: Budget Variance rose to 2.5% in 2025-Q2, up 0.4 percentage points from 2.1%, but remained green. The movement is notable because it is the largest increase so far in the sequence, even though it stays below the 3.0% threshold. Drivers appear operational rather than structural: accelerated beach-route maintenance, permit-counter temporary staffing during the spring building rush, and earlier-than-planned payments on the records-management vendor milestone. I am comfortable with the status, but I want the watch item clearly stated: second-half departments cannot treat 2.5% as extra room.
periods.recommendations: Sustain green performance by requiring midyear forecast owners to separate timing variance from true expenditure pressure in the Q2 reforecast package. Extend controls by placing a temporary Budget Office pre-review on discretionary transfers above $50,000 through September. Public Works and Community Development should submit spend-down schedules for seasonal maintenance and permit-support contracts so Q3 does not inherit avoidable noise.

periods.analysis: Budget Variance improved to 2.2% in 2025-Q3, down 0.3 percentage points from 2.5%, and stayed green. That reduction suggests the midyear controls worked: seasonal maintenance invoices caught up, temporary permit staffing tapered, and departments were more precise about accrual timing. The Finance & Administration team also appears to have benefited from the new variance-code discipline, which made the quarterly review shorter and more auditable. This is the kind of correction I want to see after a watchful Q2—measured improvement, not a sudden unexplained swing.
periods.recommendations: Keep the transfer pre-review through the end of the fiscal year, but narrow it to departments still above a 2.0% internal variance marker. Extend the successful variance-code process by adding a dashboard cut for timing, volume, and policy-driven variance categories. For Q4 close, Budget should schedule early check-ins with Parks, Public Works, and Community Development so seasonal accounts are reconciled before the final two weeks.

periods.analysis: Budget Variance reached 1.8% in 2025-Q4, down 0.4 percentage points from 2.2%, the strongest result in this series and solidly green. The year-end improvement reflects better close discipline, including earlier invoice cutoff notices to vendors such as North Coast Fleet Parts and Sentinel Software. Departments also used the Q3 dashboard to clean up low-dollar encumbrances before close rather than after Finance had to chase them. For a city managing rapid service demand, 1.8% is a strong control outcome, provided we do not let the process become personality-dependent.
periods.recommendations: Institutionalize the Q4 close calendar by publishing it as Administrative Control Memo 26-01 with named owners and due dates. Extend the green result by setting an internal management aim of 2.0% for the first half of 2026 while preserving the formal <=3.0% target. Finance should document the close procedures in a desk manual so the result survives staff turnover and audit timing pressures.

periods.analysis: Budget Variance increased to 2.1% in 2026-Q1, up 0.3 percentage points from 1.8%, while remaining green. The movement is acceptable after an unusually tight year-end close, and it aligns with Q1 reset items such as labor step increases, cybersecurity subscription renewals, and front-loaded training for the customer-service cohort at City Hall. I do not see evidence of budget drift, but the increase confirms why the new 2.0% internal management aim should be treated as a control tool, not a promise. The AA-rated posture depends on catching these small movements before they harden into base-budget expectations.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the green status by completing a Q1 payroll-to-position reconciliation for all funds before the next forecast lock. Extend the control environment by adding subscription and software renewals to the same pre-review workflow used for large transfers. Departments above the 2.0% internal aim should provide corrective timing plans, even though the public threshold remains <=3.0%.

periods.analysis: Budget Variance rose to 2.6% in 2026-Q2, up 0.5 percentage points from 2.1%, still green but now close enough to the 3.0% threshold to merit disciplined attention. The quarter reflects spring and early-summer operating pressure: lifeguard academy costs, traffic-signal maintenance on corridors HV-6 and Bayfront-2, and faster permit-inspection overtime tied to continued coastal infill activity. This is not a red flag, but it is the clearest watch point in the arc since 2025-Q2. The important fact is that Harborview remains within target; the important control question is whether Q3 brings the same corrective action we achieved last year.
periods.recommendations: Keep the result green by launching a 30-day variance containment review focused on overtime, seasonal contracts, and accelerated maintenance accounts. Extend prior-year best practice by reinstating the midyear discretionary transfer pre-review for all requests above $50,000 until Budget Variance returns nearer 2.0%. Finance should prepare a Q3 corrective bridge with named departmental actions, including inspection scheduling changes, lifeguard academy closeout, and purchase-order cleanup for signal maintenance.

periods.analysis: The available 2.6% variance is within the 3% ceiling, but leaves little room for departmental requests or capital schedule changes. This September entry carries forward the June figure; it is not a newly reconciled quarter-end result.
periods.recommendations: Reconcile departmental requests against capital payment schedules before the council packet and identify any forecast that would breach the ceiling.
